questions.q: List the five major supporting characters in "Going Places" and state one defining trait for each with a brief textual reference.
questions.a: The five major supporting characters are: (1) Jansie — practical/realistic ("Takes money, Soaf... They wouldn't make you manager straight off"), (2) Geoff — silent/mysterious ("Words had to be prized out of him like stones out of the ground"), (3) Father — dismissive/pragmatic ("This another of your wild stories?"), (4) Mother — weary/enduring ("Sophie watched her back stooped over the sink... wondered at the incongruity"), (5) Danny Casey — idealized/remote ("The prodigy. The innocent genius."). A wrong answer (e.g., listing Danny Casey as a "friend" or Geoff as "talkative") reveals the student is imposing external assumptions instead of reading textual evidence.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how Jansie functions as a foil to Sophie. Use two specific conversations from the text to support your explanation.
questions.a: Jansie acts as a foil by embodying the practical, class-determined reality that Sophie refuses to accept. In the opening conversation, Jansie reminds Sophie they are "earmarked for the biscuit factory" and that shop work "don't pay well," grounding Sophie's boutique fantasy in economic fact. Later, when Sophie claims she met Danny Casey, Jansie's reaction — "Jesus, I wish I'd have been there" — shows she treats it as exciting gossip, not a sacred secret, highlighting Sophie's need for exclusivity and romance. A wrong answer that says "Jansie is jealous of Sophie" or "Jansie doesn't understand Sophie" misses the structural point: Jansie *does* understand their shared reality; her tragedy is that she accepts it, making Sophie's refusal more poignant.

questions.q: Apply your understanding of Geoff's character to predict how he would react if Sophie told him she wanted to apply for a job at the biscuit factory. Justify your prediction with two pieces of textual evidence about Geoff's personality and behavior.
questions.a: Geoff would likely respond with silent resignation or a brief, non-committal grunt. Evidence: (1) "He said little at all, ever, voluntarily. Words had to be prized out of him like stones out of the ground" — he doesn't offer advice or opinions freely. (2) He is described as an "apprentice mechanic" who travels "to the far side of the city" and has "areas of his life about which she knew nothing" — he has already accepted the working-class trajectory Sophie rejects. He wouldn't encourage her dreams (he doesn't believe her Danny Casey story fully), but he wouldn't crush them verbally like their father. A wrong answer predicting a long lecture or enthusiastic support shows misunderstanding of Geoff's defined silence and passive acceptance of his lot.

questions.q: Analyze the contrast between Sophie's father and mother as representations of their socio-economic reality. How do their differing responses to Sophie's fantasies reveal different coping mechanisms for the same poverty?
questions.a: The father responds with aggressive dismissal ("One of these days you're going to talk yourself into a load of trouble"), using anger and ridicule to assert control over a reality he cannot change — his grimy face, shepherd's pie, and pub trips show a man numbing frustration. The mother responds with silent endurance: her "stooped back," "delicate bow" on apron strings, and sigh represent quiet absorption of hardship. The father externalizes the pressure (blames Sophie's "wild stories"); the mother internalizes it (body bent by labor). Together, they show the gendered experience of working-class poverty: male anger vs. female erasure. A wrong answer that says "both parents don't believe her" flattens the nuance — the father actively polices her imagination; the mother is too worn down to engage.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Danny Casey is not a character but a symbol." Defend your position with three textual arguments, considering both his real appearance (the match) and his imagined appearances.
questions.a: The statement is largely correct. Argument 1: Danny Casey has zero agency in the narrative — he never initiates action, speaks only in Sophie's imagination, and his real appearance is limited to a football match viewed from the stands ("Casey drove in the second goal"). Argument 2: His physical description exists only in Sophie's fantasy ("green eyes... gentle... freckled nose... teeth with gaps") — the text never describes him objectively. Argument 3: He functions as a projection screen for Sophie's desires: escape ("world rose to greet them"), romance ("he seemed lonely"), and validation ("He told me so"). The real Danny Casey is irrelevant; the *idea* of Danny Casey drives the plot. A wrong answer citing his autograph promise as "proof he's real" confuses Sophie's fabrication with textual reality — the promise occurs in her imagined arcade scene, not the real match.

questions.q: Create a 100-word diary entry from Jansie's perspective the night after Sophie tells her about meeting Danny Casey. Capture Jansie's voice, her awareness of their shared future, and her complicated feelings toward Sophie.
questions.a: A strong entry will: (1) Use colloquial language ("Soaf", "chuffed", "nosey"), (2) Show Jansie's practicality ("Factory starts in three months"), (3) Reveal tenderness beneath bluntness ("She'll get hurt, but what can I do?"), (4) Contrast her acceptance with Sophie's flight ("Me, I'll take the bus. She's waiting for a prince on a motorbike"). A weak entry makes Jansie sound like a narrator (formal English), or purely bitter ("I hate her dreams"), missing the text's portrayal of Jansie as melancholy but loyal ("I'll keep a secret, Soaf, you know that").

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of supporting characters involves examining the traits, motivations, ______, and narrative functions of characters other than the protagonist to understand how they shape the protagonist's journey, highlight central themes, and create a realistic fictional world through contrast, parallelism, or conflict.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're watching a movie where the main ______ has big dreams — who are the people around her that either pop her balloon or inflate it further?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify all major supporting characters in "Going Places" (Jansie, Geoff, Father, Mother, Derek, Danny Casey), describe their key traits with specific textual evidence, explain how each functions as a foil or mirror to Sophie, and analyze how their collective presence establishes the story's socio-economic reality and.
